newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian army chief slams rebels and gov't alike.
newsitem.headline: Colombian army chief slams rebels and gov't alike.

text.p: Colombia's military chief on Thursday defiantly rejected calls for peace talks with leftist rebels while slamming the weak central government and announcing he would run for president if asked.

Gen. Harold Bedoya spoke in an interview with the RCN radio news programme a day after business leaders heralded recent government statements about the possible opening of peace talks with Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebels as an important step forward.

The heads of the country's four top industrial groups made their views known in a letter to President Ernesto Samper, urging him to take any steps necessary to jump-start talks aimed at ending more than 30 years of war.

But Bedoya, warning that "the peace syndrome" was infecting the country, said only an "ostrich that is deaf, dumb, blind and with no sense of smell" would see the FARC as anything but an enemy to be defeated on the battlefield.

The veteran guerrilla fighter, whose reputation for tough talk and tactics could make him a formidable contender in presidential elections next year, openly defied calls from Samper for the army to stay out of politics.

He called the FARC, Latin America's largest and oldest guerrilla group, "a terrorist and drug trafficking monstrosity," peppering his remarks with references to the need to shore up the government and give its institutions, led by the military, a stronger hand to crush the FARC.

Samper was severely weakened even before he took office in 1994 by a scandal over allegations his election campaign was financed by drugs. Bedoya did not refer to that or to coup rumours at the height of the scandal last year, but he called the executive branch "extremely weak" and said peace talks could allow the FARC to ram "the law of the jungle, the law of the strongest and most violent" down Colombia's throat.

Bedoya was infuriated by talks that led to the FARC's release in Caqueta province on Sunday of 70 soldiers, 60 of whom had been held for more than nine months. The talks were what spurred the possibility of a broader negotiating process, but army leaders were enraged that the government took the unprecedented step of demilitarizing a vast area of national territory in exchange for the prisoners' release.

Bedoya appeared to border on mutiny when asked how he would respond if Samper, as commander-in-chief, ordered him to sit at a bargaining table with veteran FARC commander Manuel "Sureshot" Marulanda. "As soldiers we have a very specific task under the constitution. No one has ever told us that our functions include entering into talks with anyone," he said.
"What I propose to the Colombian people is that we join together," he added. "Because I think the time has come for us to unite and defeat these (FARC) delinquents."

Asked about graffiti spray-painted on walls across the capital promoting him as a presidential candidate, he said it was a "spontaneous" show of support for someone who is not prepared to "hand over the country to terrorists."
He said he had thought about running for the top job, adding: "I'll do anything I can to help" if asked to serve.
